In [[mathematics]] &mdash; specifically, in [[measure theory]] and [[functional analysis]] &mdash; the '''cylindrical σ-algebra'''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gine |first1=Evarist |last2=Nickl |first2=Richard |title=Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models |date=2016 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |page=16}}</ref> or '''product σ-algebra'''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Athreya |first1=Krishna |last2=Lahiri |first2=Soumendra |title=Measure Theory and Probability Theory |date=2006 |publisher=Springer |pages=202–203}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Cohn |first1=Donald |title=Measure Theory |date=2013 |publisher=Birkhauser |page=365 |edition=Second}}</ref> is a type of [[σ-algebra]] which is often used when studying [[product measure]]s or [[probability measure]]s of [[random variable]]s on [[Banach space]]s.

For a product space, the cylinder σ-algebra is the one that is [[Σ-algebra#σ-algebra generated by an arbitrary family|generated]] by [[cylinder set]]s.

In the context of a Banach space <math>X</math> and its [[dual space]] of [[continuous linear functional]]s <math>X',</math> the cylindrical σ-algebra <math>\mathfrak{A}(X,X')</math> is defined to be the coarsest σ-algebra (that is, the one with the fewest measurable sets) such that every [[continuous linear function]] on <math>X</math> is a [[measurable function]].  In general, <math>\mathfrak{A}(X,X')</math> is ''not'' the same as the [[Borel σ-algebra]] on <math>X,</math> which is the coarsest σ-algebra that contains all open subsets of <math>X.</math>

== Definition ==
Consider two [[topological vector space]]s <math>N</math> and <math>M</math> with [[Dual system|dual pairing]] <math>\langle,\rangle:=\langle,\rangle_{N,M}</math>, then we can define the so called [[Borel algebra|Borel]] cylinder sets
:<math>C_{f_1,\dots,f_m,B}=\{x\in N\colon (\langle x,f_1\rangle,\dots,\langle x,f_m\rangle)\in B\}</math>
for some <math>f_1,\dots,f_m\in M</math> and <math>B\in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^m)</math>. The family of all these sets is denoted as <math>\mathfrak{A}_{f_1,\dots,f_n}</math>.
Then 
:<math>\operatorname{Cyl}(N,M)=\bigotimes_n \mathfrak{A}_{f_1,\dots,f_n}</math>
is called the '''cylindrical algebra'''. Equivalently one can also look at the open cylinder sets and get the same algebra.

The '''cylindrical σ-algebra''' <math>\mathfrak{A}(N,M)=\sigma(\operatorname{Cyl}(N,M))</math> is the σ-algebra generated by the cylindrical algebra.<ref>{{citation|author=Richard M. Dudley, Jacob Feldman und [[Lucien Le Cam]] |date=1971 |editor=Princeton University |issue=2 |pages=390-392 |periodical=Annals of Mathematics |title=On Seminorms and Probabilities, and Abstract Wiener Spaces |volume=93}}</ref>

== Properties ==
* Let <math>X</math> a Hausdorff locally convex space which is also a hereditarily [[Lindelöf space]], then
::<math>\mathfrak{A}(X,X')=\mathcal{B}(X).</math><ref>{{cite journal|first1=Itaru |last1=Mitoma |first2=Susumu |last2=Okada |first3=Yoshiaki |last3=Okazaki |publisher=Osaka University and Osaka Metropolitan University, Departments of Mathematics |title=Cylindrical σ-algebra and cylindrical measure |journal=Osaka Journal of Mathematics |volume=14 |number=3 |date=1977 |page=640}} </ref>
